title: Vox PopulAI: Lessons from a global law firm's exploration of generative AI
author: Ashurst LLP (Office of the Chief Digital Officer)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Ashurst’s firm-wide trials substantiate the cluster’s core proposition with concrete deployment evidence: generative AI delivered measurable gains on bounded drafting and meeting-support tasks, while frequent hallucinations required human verification. The source also strengthens the organisational-complements point by treating training and support as essential to capability-building rather than assuming tool access alone creates value.

kp.k: Global trials combined experiments, blind assessment and staff feedback
kp.d: Ashurst reports three global GenAI trials led by its Office of the Chief Digital Officer from November 2023 to March 2024, involving 411 partners, lawyers and staff across 23 offices in 14 countries. Outcomes used publicly available data, not client data, under guardrails. The methodology combined surveys, controlled experiments and a blind comparison of UK case summaries. Four expertise lawyers across three practice areas suggested four cases of varying length and complexity; output was anonymised to remove formatting clues. Approximately 25% of participants undertook at least one structured experiment alongside independent exploration.

kp.k: First drafting offered the strongest initial legal value
kp.d: Ashurst identifies faster first drafts, including collecting and understanding source material, as GenAI’s greatest initial legal value. An average of 77% of post-trial survey respondents agreed or strongly agreed that GenAI helped them reach a first draft faster. Controlled experiments measured approximate time savings of 80% for UK corporate filings involving articles of association, 59% for industry/sector-specific research reports using public company Form 10-K filings, and 45% for first-draft legal briefings. Participants valued having a rough draft to reshape rather than starting from a blank page.

kp.k: Nonlegal drafting and meeting support also saved time
kp.d: Controlled experiments on job descriptions, policy documents and social media posts measured approximate savings of up to two hours per participant per task, with very high overall quality scores relative to legal content. In an open experiment, 21 participants used GenAI for meeting summaries, recaps and action points, reporting circa 10 minutes saved per 30-minute call on average; output averaged 3.8/5. Participants said reduced note-taking allowed greater presence in meetings. These findings concern particular trial tasks rather than firm-wide productivity.

kp.k: Accuracy varied more widely than human first drafts
kp.d: In the blind case-summary study, GenAI accuracy scores ranged from 1 to 4 out of 5, compared with 3 to 4 for human first drafts; average scores were 3 and 3.5 respectively. In 67% of cases, GenAI output matched or exceeded human output’s accuracy score. Experts correctly identified all human outputs, but 50% of GenAI outputs were either mistaken for human work or could not be classified. Ashurst treats language, tone, structure, judgment and broader legal analysis as possible indicators of authorship, not established universal tests.

kp.k: Expert verification conditions any potential productivity gains
kp.d: Ashurst cautions that inaccurate initial output can send a drafter down the wrong path and increase correction time, so faster drafting does not necessarily produce net savings. It requires thorough review by appropriate experts. Participants reported frequent hallucinations across all trialled tools, supporting a human-in-the-loop approach even where participants used GenAI as a sense check or second pair of eyes. Freeing lawyers for higher-value work or development, and accelerating delivery to clients, are presented as potential consequences rather than demonstrated downstream outcomes.

kp.k: Legal quality requires numerical assessment and subjective judgment
kp.d: Ashurst assessed accuracy, appropriateness, completeness, usability and confidence, each out of five, but concluded that quality could not be captured adequately by averaging scores. Expert preferences differed over grammar, comprehensiveness and vocabulary, although differing cases and complexity could also explain those differences. One expert rejected output containing a hallucinated, incorrect verdict and scored every criterion 1/5. Other participants tolerated errors they expected review to catch. In another experiment, material scored 2/5 for usability and saved no legal time, yet its user still recommended GenAI based on other experiences. Overall, 67% of post-trial survey respondents recommended onboarding the associated tool despite criticisms.

kp.k: Staff perceived workload support and greater future preparedness
kp.d: Across legal, consulting and business-services personnel, trial feedback identified support benefits beyond task speed. Of post-trial survey respondents, 61% agreed that the relevant tool would help them feel more supported in managing their workload. One participant valued assistance when colleagues were offline, subject to subsequent checking with a colleague. At the end of the biggest trial, 88% of respondents said GenAI helped them feel more prepared for the future. These are reported perceptions, not measured reductions in workload or demonstrated future capability.

kp.k: Adoption requires sustained learning, not merely tool access
kp.d: Drawing on the cited jagged technological frontier framework, Ashurst reports uneven task performance and argues that mapping use cases or providing intuitive tools is insufficient. Even tasks thought to be within the frontier did not reliably yield legally correct, high-quality output; frustration and discouragement were important adoption risks. Hands-on experimentation and continuing dialogue revealed where GenAI added value, clarified lawyers’ own contribution when it failed, and exposed wider technical and soft-skills development needs. Recommendations include diverse trial participants, knowledgeable trial leads, collaborative feedback, application-focused demonstrations and time-bound trials with friendly competition.

kp.k: Trial findings do not establish business-model transformation
kp.d: Ashurst explicitly warns that the sample size prevents straightforward extrapolation to definitive firm-wide time and cost savings. Its view in this 2024 report is that the industry remains some years away from determining or implementing necessary law-firm business-model changes directly attributable to GenAI adoption. The trials informed investment decisions, policy design and implementation, but the report presents provisional learning rather than complete findings and calls for more testing of complex work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ashurst identifies first-draft assistance as GenAI’s principal initial legal benefit, while reporting uneven accuracy, broader staff benefits and substantial adoption requirements.
pts.d: Ashurst claims that GenAI accelerates first drafts and the collection and understanding of supporting material, helping lawyers overcome a blank page. It predicts that this could free drafters for higher-value work or development and deliver drafts to reviewers and ultimately clients sooner; these are potential workflow consequences rather than measured firm-wide outcomes. Its blind study found that AI case summaries could be difficult to distinguish from human summaries when legally correct, although human work had higher average accuracy and AI accuracy varied more widely. Ashurst also concludes that assessing legal quality requires subjective commentary as well as numerical scores. Beyond legal drafting, the report identifies benefits in non-legal content creation, meeting summaries, workload support and staff preparedness. Some participants treated AI as a second pair of eyes or an out-of-hours assistant, but Ashurst maintains that human checking is necessary. Finally, Ashurst argues that identifying use cases and providing easy-to-use tools are insufficient: realising value requires hands-on experience, ongoing dialogue, training and organisational support. Its business-model prediction is cautious: the industry remains some years away from determining or implementing necessary changes directly attributable to GenAI adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw on Ashurst’s own three global trials, combining a small blind comparison, controlled and open experiments, surveys and participant commentary.
pts.d: The trials involved 411 partners, lawyers and staff across 23 offices in 14 countries. Approximately 25% participated in at least one structured experiment alongside independent exploration. The blind study compared anonymised UK case summaries using four cases proposed by four expertise lawyers across three practice areas. Controlled experiments reported approximate drafting time savings of 80% for UK corporate filings, 59% for industry/sector research reports drawing on public company filings and 45% for legal briefings. An average of 77% of post-trial survey respondents agreed or strongly agreed that GenAI helped them reach a first draft faster. Non-legal drafting experiments reported savings of up to two hours per participant per task. In the blind study, AI accuracy scores ranged from 1 to 4 out of 5, versus 3 to 4 for human drafts; averages were 3 and 3.5 respectively. AI matched or exceeded human accuracy scores in 67% of cases, while 50% of AI outputs were either mistaken for human work or could not be classified. All human outputs were correctly identified. Quality-related evidence includes divergent reviewer preferences, an AI-generated incorrect verdict that prompted uniformly critical scoring, and participants who remained positive despite unusable output or errors. In an open meeting experiment involving 21 participants, reported savings averaged about 10 minutes per 30-minute call, with an average output score of 3.8/5. Post-trial survey findings included 61% expecting better workload support and, in the largest trial, 88% feeling more prepared for the future. These are reported perceptions, task-level measurements and qualitative observations, not demonstrated firm-wide savings. External references provide background: Linklaters’ English-law benchmark on reliability, Better Call GPT on task performance, and Dell’Acqua and colleagues on the jagged technological frontier.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern November 2023–March 2024 trials; productivity benefits depend on correctness, expert review and supported adoption, and cannot establish definitive business-model effects.
pts.d: The 2024 report presents early findings from trials conducted between November 2023 and March 2024, not mature or universal capability claims. Outcomes used publicly available rather than client data and were subject to guardrails. Ashurst conditions time savings on legal correctness: an incorrect initial steer can send a drafter down the wrong path and increase subsequent correction time. The report therefore requires appropriate expert review and retains humans in the loop, citing participant reports of frequent hallucinations across all tools trialled without supplying a measured hallucination rate. Even tasks considered within AI’s capability frontier did not reliably produce high-quality, legally correct work. The report explicitly cautions against extrapolating its sample to definitive firm-wide time or cost savings. Its expectation that business-model changes remain some years away is an undated forward-looking judgment from 2024, rather than a quantified forecast. More-complex work requires further testing, and adoption depends on sustained learning, dialogue, support and attention to users’ needs.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are lawyers and staff within a global law firm, their reviewers, firm leadership and potentially clients receiving faster services.
pts.d: Lawyers drafting filings, briefings, research reports and case summaries may gain faster starting points and assistance gathering material, but remain responsible for checking and reshaping outputs. Reviewers may receive drafts sooner while retaining expert verification responsibilities. Consulting personnel and business services professionals may benefit from drafting job descriptions, policies and social content, as well as meeting recaps and action lists. Staff report greater workload support and preparedness, including assistance outside normal working hours that still requires later colleague checking. Digital, knowledge, learning and development, risk and information-security teams face new responsibilities for training, governance, evaluation and supported implementation. Firm leadership gains evidence for technology investment and policy decisions, but the report does not establish aggregate savings or immediate changes to pricing, staffing or business models. Clients could benefit from faster delivery and more direct attention, but these benefits are prospective because the trials did not use client data. The report offers lessons for other organisations without claiming demonstrated effects on entry-level employment, ALSP competition or access to justice.
